detail.abstract: Outsourcing companies play a significant role in reducing youth unemployment. However, many young university graduates find themselves in positions that are not aligned with their education or skills. In Romania’s business service sector, graduates face complex challenges; however, little is known about the precarious career paths they encounter in entry-level outsourced jobs. This qualitative research, based on a 2-year ethnographic case study, provides insights into the factors contributing to job precarity and describes its defining features. Through reflexive thematic analysis, this study examines this issue comprehensively and discusses the complicity of employees in managerial roles while questioning the validity of job promises made by outsourced organizations, particularly as entry-level customer support representatives (CSRs) employees experience precarity. These findings indicate that inadequate work environments lead to deskilling and an increase in emotional labor. This study reveals that financial incentives do not keep pace with the demands for deep- or surface-acting emotions in outsourced contexts. This underscores the importance of Arlie Russell Hochschild’s influential work by providing a thorough examination of emotional labor and its implications for CSRs. The study concludes with a call for urgent policy changes to strengthen the link between higher education, the labor market, and prospects for a decent career for university graduates.

title: Incentives for Redeveloping Multi-Family Buildings: The Role of Eminent Domain and Density Regulation

detail.title: Incentives for Redeveloping Multi-Family Buildings: The Role of Eminent Domain and Density Regulation
detail.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the role of eminent domain and density regulation in providing incentives for redevelopment of multi-family buildings. With ownership dispersed vertically, the prerequisite consolidation is hampered by negotiation frictions and density restrictions, resulting in weak incentives in the private sector. Theoretically, we document that eminent domain and density regulation modify the option value of redevelopment and generate positive extensive and intensive margin effects on redevelopment probability. Empirically, we utilize a regression discontinuity design using building-age-based threshold reduction to assess the impacts of eminent domain. The finding reveals that a reduction in the threshold for eminent domain from 90% to 80% increases redevelopment probability by 2%. A spatial regression discontinuity design using area-based relaxation is conducted to assess the impacts of density regulation, suggesting that a 20% density relaxation leads to a 9% increase in redevelopment probability.

title: Land Demarcation and the Geography of Urban Redevelopment: Evidence from Land Assembly In Hong Kong

detail.title: Land Demarcation and the Geography of Urban Redevelopment: Evidence from Land Assembly In Hong Kong
detail.abstract: Urban redevelopment demands efficient land assembly, shaped by the land demarcation system. This paper exploits the cession of Hong Kong and survey-based land administration during the British colonial era to identify how lot shape complexity and land use variance affect holdouts in land assembly in present Hong Kong. Using natural geographic constraints and historical planning barriers as instruments, we find that lot shape complexity lowers assembly probability along with reduced scale, prolonged duration, and inflated cost due to spatial frictions and ambiguous property rights. Land use variance, despite incurring delays in planning approvals, promotes land assembly probability through flexibility-induced premium.

title: The Economics of Urban Redevelopment: Price Gradient, Spatial Structure, And Spillover
affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: The Economics of Urban Redevelopment: Price Gradient, Spatial Structure, And Spillover
detail.abstract: Studies on the economics of urban redevelopment face identification challenges due to the nonrandom assignment inherent in place-based policies. In this paper, we leverage a discontinuity design rooted in Hong Kong's eminent domain policy for private-led redevelopment projects targeting buildings aged 50 years and above. Using this quasi-random assignment of redevelopment incentives, we employ a shift-share IV approach that capitalizes on communitylevel geographic variation in building age composition, combined with granular spatiotemporal data to isolate intra-city effects. Our findings reveal that redevelopment leads to a spatial leveling of price gradients: rental prices flatten by 10.7% to 16.2%, property transactions by 4.9% to 12.1%, and land leases by 35.7% to 39.3%. This leveling generates positive spillovers on urban structure, including enhanced business agglomeration and intensified job opportunities, without evidence of displacement-driven outcomes. Notably, while agglomeration intensifies, gentrification and segregation effects are limited, suggesting that these gains are achieved without incurring the typical costs associated with redevelopment.

detail.abstract: Does making green identity salient increase pro-environmental choices in the circular economy? This question has largely been explored through studies with single goods in a small number of Western societies. We explore possible answers to this question, we conduct an experiment with 985 participants in Japan, designed to test the effects of identity reinforcement and product labelling on pro-environmental financial decision makings. Participants who pass a minimal test of environmentally friendly activity (e.g. sorting household waste) are randomly assigned to receive the identity label as "Environmentally Conscious Consumers". The label is visible to participants themselves in the treatment group throughout the experiment to reinforce environmental identity. After an incentivized task used as a manipulation check, participants make 10 hypothetical choices about minimum acceptable discounts for circular products (repaired, reused or recycled). In some cases, the circular product has a prominent and attractive sticker enabling that the user could be 'seen to be green.' In common with previous results, attaching a label to an individual raises their valuation of the environmental goods, in the sense that the required discount is lower for treated individuals. On the other hand, adding labels to goods such as 'recycled' or 'repaired' raises the discount required compared to matched, but unlabelled green products. Subjects of all types and ages are antipathetic to the labelled good. This is in strong contrast to results found in other countries and suggests that 'green to be seen' and similar messages may not apply in cultures where norms are against the public signalling of pro-social behaviour.

title: Better Listening through Seeing? Origins and Solutions to Multimodal Cognitive Conflict in AI-Generated Visuals
affiliations: , Southern University of Science and Technology, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business and Arizona State University, W. P. Carey School of Business

detail.title: Better Listening through Seeing? Origins and Solutions to Multimodal Cognitive Conflict in AI-Generated Visuals
detail.abstract: Firms have started to invest intensively in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to automate workflows, reduce costs, and achieve scalable operations. Yet, despite its promise, the operational effectiveness of GenAI remains uncertain, particularly for multimodal output that may interact directly with end users. We conceptualize and empirically validate a novel operational risk of adoption-multimodal cognitive conflict-which arises when AI-generated visuals are visually salient but semantically misaligned with task content, thereby disrupting user cognitive processing and impairing performance. Drawing on the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML), we develop a theory-driven prompt engineering framework to mitigate this risk by aligning generative outputs with human cognition. We test this framework in a randomized field experiment on an online learning platform, where students complete dictation task with multimodal interaction. This context is operationally ideal as the platform faces resource constraints, making automated visual generation appealing but risky. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: no visuals (control), naïve GenAI-generated visuals, or theory-driven GenAI-generated visuals. Results show that naïve visuals reduced practice intensity and impaired dictation performance without improving monetization. In contrast, theory-driven visuals increased practice attempts by 29.9%, improved learning performance, and raised average user payments by 23.23 RMB. Our study contributes by introducing the origins of a new operational risk in multimodal GenAI adoption, proposing a theory-driven solution, and validating it through a field experiment.

detail.title: The Effect of Online Fitness Challenges on Channel Performance and User Engagement
detail.abstract: Despite the boom of the fitness industry and recent technological developments that enhance physical activity, individuals still experience barriers to consistent exercise. Recently, the online fitness market has expanded through the growing popularity of fitness apps and online workouts posted on social media. One way that these fitness creators have kept their audience engaged is fitness challenges, that is, a workout plan published by a creator with defined start and end dates. We use the context of YouTube yoga channels to estimate the effect of such challenges on the performance of the hosting channels and their followers' activity during and after the challenges. We collect data for yoga channels on YouTube and estimate the impact of holding fitness challenges. We demonstrate that fitness challenges improve aggregate channel performance, such as daily views and engagements, both during and after a challenge. Further, we extend the selfdetermination theory and analyze user comments content to find that holding challenges helps improve motivation to exercise by enhancing individuals' feeling of competence and relatedness. Finally, we find that the positive effects of holding fitness challenges on channel performance are stronger for smaller channels with fewer followers and less mature channels with shorter tenure and shorter prior activity history. Overall, our findings suggest that fitness challenges can be an efficient strategy for fitness workout creators to improve their channel performance and for content consumers to increase engagement. The findings have several important implications for fitness content creators, consumers, sponsors, and policymakers.

detail.title: Proposing a Design Theory for a Human-Learning-Guided Virtual Negotiator for Online Trading Platforms
detail.abstract: Negotiation-based transactional mechanisms provide flexibility and economic benefits to both sellers and buyers on online trading platforms. Although automated negotiation is a highly desired feature among online platform providers, the complexity and un- certainty of human behavior in human-to-computer (HtC) negotiation make it a problematic solution. This study proposes a design theory for a human-learning guided virtual negotiator (HLG-VN) framework that emulates human learning using multiple machine learning (ML) techniques that collectively mimic four human learning activities: didactic, feedback, observational, and analogical learning. Fol- lowing the design science research methodology, we built an instantiation system for the proposed design theory and empirically tested it using experiments based on HtC negotiations. The empirical results show that our system outperformed the benchmark system in terms of both economic and some key social-psychological outcomes. Furthermore, the experiment results confirm the effectiveness and cor- rectness of the HLG-VN framework. The proposed design theory provides a theoretical base for using ML techniques to build a virtual negotiator agent for an automated negotiation system. Thus, various agents could be designed and developed based on the theory for online trading platforms, thus improving negotiation efficiency and reducing transaction costs.

detail.title: Is nurse clinical decision-making supported by digital developments? The nursing process examined using a pre and post digital health information system record audit
detail.abstract: Background The nursing process (Assessment, Planning, Intervention, and Outcome) is fundamental to nurse decision-making and care. Given recent increases in the use of Digital Health Information Systems (DHIS) there is an opportunity to maximise nursing efficiency and patient safety.MethodsA retrospective clinical record audit to evaluate completeness of nursing process documentation was undertaken. The study occurred pre (hybrid - a paper and digital system, in mid-2022) and post (digital system, mid-2023) implementation of a DHIS. Retrospective records (N=240) of a randomised sample of medical patients admitted to an Australian metropolitan tertiary teaching hospital for longer than 48 hours were examined.ResultsNursing Assessment, Planning and Intervention were more complete in the DHIS (p<0.001). Outcome was documented similarly in both groups, but the hybrid system mean was higher than DHIS (p=0.17). Information retrieval time was higher in DHIS (mean=19.0 minutes) compared to the hybrid system (mean=9.40 minutes).ConclusionDHIS demonstrated improved completeness of information to support nurse decision-making. However, it took twice as long to retrieve this increased information content. Neither hybrid nor digital records performed well in capturing Outcomes, which could be influenced by workload and accessibility of data from previous shifts. This current evidence indicates nurses are collecting more data than they use to evaluate the quality and effectiveness of care provided. Future research can focus on retrievability of information and whether duplication and repetition of comprehensive assessments are contributing to missed nursing care.

title: Are Negative Reviews always Helpful? Effects of Emotional Arousal on the Usefulness of Negative Reviews and How Merchants should Respond

detail.title: Are Negative Reviews always Helpful? Effects of Emotional Arousal on the Usefulness of Negative Reviews and How Merchants should Respond
detail.abstract: In the rapidly evolving digital marketplace, understanding consumer behavior in response to negative reviews is of considerable practical and academic importance. Negative reviews influence consumer decision-making, but not all are accurate or helpful. Moreover, the interplay between emotional arousal and the perceived utility of negative reviews, particularly for high-risk purchases and costly products, remains largely unexplored. Addressing this gap, our study leverages attribution theory to scrutinize the curvilinear relationship between emotional arousal and the usefulness of negative reviews in high-risk purchases. We employed a robust mixed-methods design comprising three different studies aimed to triangulate further and understand these phenomena: Study 1 involved an objective content analysis of 6,147 negative reviews from prominent Chinese e-commerce platforms; Study 2 was a controlled scenario-based experiment with 99 consumers, aimed to test the underlying causal relationships; finally, Study 3 involved in-depth qualitative interviews and coding with 60 consumers. Our findings demonstrate an inverted U-shaped relationship between emotional arousal and the perceived utility of negative reviews in high-risk purchase scenarios. This relationship is mediated by prosocial motives, emphasizing that emotionally aroused consumers will likely find negative reviews helpful only up to a certain point, after which the utility diminishes. Notably, positive merchant responses serve as a crucial moderating variable in the emotional arousal-negative review usefulness relationship and the connection between prosocial motives and review usefulness. Our study advances the online review literature by offering nuanced insights into the complex relationship between emotional arousal and the utility of negative reviews in high-risk purchase scenarios. Our results have immediate implications for e-commerce platforms, enabling them to convert the challenge posed by negative reviews into actionable opportunities through informed response strategies.

title: Enterprise Risk Management as Strategy

detail.title: Enterprise Risk Management as Strategy
detail.abstract: This paper explores the integration of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) into organizational strategy as a response to volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) environments. Drawing on established frameworks such as COSO (2017) and ISO 31000, the study examines governance structures, risk appetite statements, scenario analysis, stress testing, and key risk indicators as mechanisms that support ERM adoption. Case studies from the mining, construction, and energy sectors highlight how ERM enhances resilience, guides sustainability transitions, and supports innovation. The analysis finds that while ERM should not be considered a strategy, it is a critical enabler of strategic success by equipping organizations with tools, culture, and governance to balance opportunity with risk. The paper concludes that ERM is a dynamic capability that strengthens organizational adaptability, resilience, and long-term value creation.

title: Gaps in LLM Awareness, Usage, and Perceptions in the United States: Evidence from a Nationally Representative Longitudinal Survey
affiliations: , , University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Gaps in LLM Awareness, Usage, and Perceptions in the United States: Evidence from a Nationally Representative Longitudinal Survey

publicationDetails.journalName: USC Center for Economic & Social Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to benefit users both in their work and personal lives, but what groups are quickest to adopt them? To investigate awareness, usage and perception of LLMs across socio-demographic groups-and track changes over time-we administered a two-wave survey using a nationally representative, probability-based online panel of 12,224 U.S. residents. Across two survey waves spanning one year, we observed marked gaps in usage: groups more likely to use LLMs included men, younger adults, those with college education, higher incomes, those in more analytical occupations (e.g., STEM), Democrats, and those with above-median cognitive ability, internet literacy, and openness to new experience. These usage gaps do not appear to be declining and, in many cases, seem to be widening over time. Our analyses indicate that these disparities are associated with differences in both access-related factors (e.g., income, occupation, digital skills) and attitudes (e.g., perceived usefulness of LLMs). Our data provide a dynamic understanding of the rapidly evolving exposure to, adoption of, and attitudes toward LLMs in the U.S. population.

title: When the Gates Open: Ghost Month and the Hauntings of the Web
affiliations: Falmouth University

detail.title: When the Gates Open: Ghost Month and the Hauntings of the Web
detail.abstract: At its core, Ghost Month is about infrastructures of connection. The gates of the underworld are said to swing open, allowing for traffic (spiritual, emotional, social) between realms. It is about networks: between the living and the dead and also between generations, between households and temples, between earthly desires and cosmic orders. And here is where I want to ask: what if we read the internet itself as a kind of ghost gate? What if the lag, glitches, hidden circuits of our digital infrastructures are not simply “errors” but hauntings, reminders that our networks, too, are spectral spaces where living and nonliving, human and machinic, constantly mingle?

title: From Labels to Behaviors: Temporal and Spillover Effects of Crowdsourced Fact-Checking
affiliations: Georgia State University - Department of Computer Information Systems, , Texas Tech University - Rawls College of Business and Arizona State University (ASU) - Department of Information Systems

detail.title: From Labels to Behaviors: Temporal and Spillover Effects of Crowdsourced Fact-Checking
detail.abstract: Crowdsourced fact-checking, where users collaboratively label or flag potential misinformation content, has been increasingly used on online platforms to combat misinformation. However, its practical effectiveness remains unclear. This study evaluates its effectiveness across two key dimensions: content scope and time horizon, by examining spillover effects across content and temporal effects over both shortand long-term periods. Using the context of Twitter's Community Notes program, this study investigates the impacts of crowdsourced fact-checking on: (1) audience engagement with labeled authors and (2) labeled authors' content generation. Our findings reveal that community notes reduce audience engagement with labeled authors' subsequent unlabeled content, likely because these notes act as a negative signal that undermines audience perception of the labeled authors' credibility and social image. This audience disengagement effect is more pronounced for authors with lower popularity, suggesting crowdsourced factchecking's limited impact on disciplining popular authors. Additionally, labeled authors decrease the volume of their future posts, although their effort invested in each post remained largely unchanged. These findings highlight the effectiveness of crowdsourced fact-checking in two aspects: (1) reducing audience engagement with labeled information sources and (2) fostering a degree of self-discipline in labeled authors' content generation, while also revealing a key boundary condition-author popularity-that shapes these effects. This study contributes to the theoretical understanding of the effectiveness of crowdsourced factchecking and provides practical insights for platforms seeking to curb misinformation.

Against the backdrop of these factual and normative developments, three Max Planck Institutes decided to jointly set up the humanet3 group which analyzes, deconstructs, and reimagines the ‘human-centered digital transformation’ of digital public spaces. title: Environmental protection and supply chain management in Vietnam
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Drexel University

detail.title: Environmental protection and supply chain management in Vietnam
detail.abstract: Adverse environmental impacts in Vietnam are caused by supply chain distortions of the bullwhip effect, and an objective of our study was to employ a qualitative and quantitative MMNCAES to minimize bullwhip data effects on Vietnam’s environmental protection’s barriers. This integrated approach for providing optimization of both environmental protection and supply chain management data in our model was not observed in the reviewed literature. Using these approaches, this paper suggests that Vietnam can meet demand expectations without a bullwhip effect. However, the adverse environmental impacts are expected to continue to affect Vietnam’s supply chain management. Various scenarios range from disruptions in the water cycle affecting agriculture to insufficient environmental protection policies. We developed a research question, initiated model building, hypothesis testing, a literature review and data gathering of 527 data points from 30 firms in Vietnam, to study the case of the bullwhip phenomenon under information technology and environmental disruptions and potential post COVID and climate change de-globalization effects (Free and Hecimovic; 2021). We posit that post COVID de-globalization will exacerbate these effects on the Vietnam supply chain. Lack of river access for mass irrigation will lead to reductions of rice output per acre. This impact may lead to the bullwhip effect being less relevant as Vietnam and the world struggle to meet supply rather than overestimated demand in the new de-globalization era. Quantitative crosstab analysis showed that sales could be improved relative to demand.

title: Carrier Tension in Leadership Fields - Counterstructure to Ekpathic Rhetoric
affiliations: Orto Lab - Reflexive Intelligence & Future Strategy

detail.title: Carrier Tension in Leadership Fields - Counterstructure to Ekpathic Rhetoric
detail.abstract:
This paper explores the architecture of leadership beyond methods and models. It introduces the concept of carrier tension as a structural condition that enables systems to hold unresolved proximity–distance dynamics without collapsing into simplification or overreaction.

In the current discourse, leadership is increasingly framed through empathy or its counterpart, ekpathy – both presented as tools of clarity and optimization. This paper questions that framing. It does not offer correction, but an alternative perspective: leadership as an architectural performance under semantic pressure.

Using examples from organizational theory, systems thinking, and epistemic philosophy, the work traces how resonance without tension leads to simulation, and how structures can remain intact even when certainty is no longer available.

The aim is not to replace existing models, but to introduce a new axis of reflection. Leadership, here, is understood not as a style, nor as a function – but as a held form under load.

This paper is an invitation: to pause certainty, to explore tension, and to ask what leadership becomes when answers are no longer sufficient – but presence is still required.

title: House M.D. As A Lens to Explore Antisocial Leadership Traits in Organisational Behaviour
affiliations: Westford University

detail.title: House M.D. As A Lens to Explore Antisocial Leadership Traits in Organisational Behaviour
detail.abstract: This essay examines the fictional workplace of House M.D. through the lens of Organisational Behaviour (OB) and Human Resource (HR) management, with emphasis on toxic leadership and workplace culture. Dr. Gregory House, an exceptional diagnostician with limited interpersonal skills, exhibits traits consistent with antisocial personality disorder (ASPD), including manipulation, lack of empathy, and disregard for rules. These behaviours foster a toxic environment that normalises unethical practices and erodes psychological safety, echoing real organisations that tolerate disruptive yet high-performing employees. Drawing on frameworks such as Schein's organisational culture model, task versus relational performance, and team development theory, the analysis explores how House's leadership undermines trust, communication, and collaboration. A comparison with Amazon's demanding corporate culture illustrates how fiction mirrors real-world organisational challenges, and how fictional case studies create a space for applying OB theories, where students can critically analyse morally ambiguous scenarios, like that of House M.D. Ultimately, the essay underscores the need to recognise early warning signs, promote ethical leadership, and balance productivity with employee well-being to sustain healthy organisational cultures.

title: Quantifying Decoupling in Global Production and Trade
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, Yale University and City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: Quantifying Decoupling in Global Production and Trade
detail.abstract: We analyze the fragmentation of the global economy into competing blocs through both trade and multinational production channels. Combining a multi-country semiendogenous growth model with bilateral flow data, we document how countries sort into US-and China-centered blocs. We uncover an asymmetry: multinational production alignments reflect economic fundamentals while trade alignments deviate from welfare-maximizing configurations. Countries maintain split alignments-producing with one bloc while trading with another-at substantial economic cost. Production decoupling generates larger welfare losses than trade fragmentation by disrupting technology diffusion, the primary channel through which multinational production affects long-term growth. Developing economies benefit from bloc consolidation through technology access; developed economies lose from realignment. These costs of fragmentation extend beyond trade diversion to reshape global technology diffusion and growth trajectories.

title: Sustainable and Resilient Supply Chain Strategies in the Post-COVID Era
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Sustainable and Resilient Supply Chain Strategies in the Post-COVID Era
detail.abstract: This study examines the critical vulnerabilities exposed in global supply chains by the COVID-19 pandemic, emphasizing the intertwined nature of sustainability and resilience as strategic priorities. It explores foundational concepts of sustainable supply chain management, including the triple bottom line framework and the integration of environmental, social, and economic objectives. The analysis covers historical shifts from localized to globalized supply networks, highlighting the challenges posed by increased complexity and the role of digital transformation in enhancing transparency and adaptability. The pandemic's multifaceted impacts across sectors such as food, manufacturing, healthcare, and retail are assessed, with attention to supply-demand shocks, logistics disruptions, workforce effects, and sustainability challenges. The paper proposes strategic adaptations including risk assessment, agility, redundancy, and diversification, alongside innovations in circular economy practices, green technologies, and product design. It further discusses the integration of sustainability and resilience through systems thinking, network theory, and socio-ecological perspectives, emphasizing governance, collaboration, and performance measurement. Barriers such as organizational culture, resource constraints, and regulatory complexities are addressed, with consideration of regional differences between developed and developing economies. The role of international trade policies, certification systems, transparency initiatives, and public-private partnerships in advancing sustainable and resilient supply chains is explored. Finally, emerging trends in bio-based materials, decentralized manufacturing, carbon neutrality, and consumer engagement are presented as pathways for future transformation. The study underscores the necessity of coordinated, multi-stakeholder approaches to build supply chains capable of withstanding disruptions while advancing environmental stewardship and social equity.

title: When Data Protection Backfires: Consumer Data Shielding in Algorithmic Personalized Pricing
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), affiliation not provided to SSRN, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: When Data Protection Backfires: Consumer Data Shielding in Algorithmic Personalized Pricing
detail.abstract: Advances in big data and machine learning have enabled firms to implement algorithmic personalized pricing based on consumer data. However, in response to growing fairness concerns, consumers are increasingly engaging in data shielding behaviors-such as disabling cookies and using privacy-focused browsers-to avoid price discrimination. This study develops a stylized model to examine how data shielding, driven by fairness concerns and shielding costs, interacts with firms' pricing strategies and affects firm profitability, consumer surplus, and social welfare. Our findings offer several intriguing insights. First, although data shielding might seem to counter personalized pricing, it can unexpectedly benefit firm profits. As more consumers shield their data, the uniform pricing segment expands, enhancing firms' market power and allowing them to raise uniform prices with less competitive pressure. The higher uniform prices, in turn, elevate personalized prices without triggering consumer switching-creating a reinforcing dynamic that enhances overall profitability. Second, we find that even if data shielding is costless, it can harm consumer surplus when firms hold substantial exclusive data. Data shielding improves consumer surplus only when firms have limited exclusive data and shielding costs are sufficiently low. Finally, we show that consumers can be better off with algorithmic personalized pricing than uniform pricing, particularly when data shielding costs are relatively high and fairness concerns are low. Overall, these findings caution that one-size-fits-all data protection policies may backfire on consumers, and highlight the need to tailor such policies to market-specific factors such as data exclusivity and fairness concern levels.

title: Machine Predictions and Causal Explanations: Evidence from a Field Experiment
affiliations: Vanderbilt University and INSEAD

detail.title: Machine Predictions and Causal Explanations: Evidence from a Field Experiment
detail.abstract: A key role that decision-makers play in organizations is to provide causal explanations for decisions. Yet despite growing evidence on how machine predictions impact decisions, there has been less insight on how they affect decision-makers' ability to explain and reason through their decisions. We explore this question in this paper, using a field experiment we designed and ran across mutual fund analysts in a leading investment research firm. We randomly assigned analysts to receive predictions for fund ratings based on a proprietary machine learning algorithm developed within the company, and observed their decisions and causal explanations for those decisions over 6 months. We find that even when predictions improve decisions, they can worsen the reasoning of the causal explanations that decision-makers provide for their decisions. Inexperienced analysts working on simpler decisions are especially affected, leading them to provide worse explanations when working with machine predictions. These findings suggest that the growing use of AI may accrue knowledge without understanding, especially hindering inexperienced decision-makers from developing expertise.

title: Multi-Sensor Data Fusion (MSDF) in AI Public Policy
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: Multi-Sensor Data Fusion (MSDF) in AI Public Policy
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) can mean many different things, e.g., formalizing ontologies, building/testing expert systems, robotics refinement and deployment, machine learning (ML), neural networks. However, increasingly AI produces anxiety over hallucinations, human worker displacement, sentience and singularity. At this moment, public policy confronts a host of AI’s negative externalities while it balances these side effects against the transformative promise that AI proponents regularly claim. Much of this seems mere hopeful aspiration. Moore’s law adds both negative and positive weight to projections that computing resources and computational capacities will continue expanding logarithmically making AI advancements feasible as AI is poised to expand in the medium term. Predictably, AI progress will also be influenced by quantum computing. Regulatory guardrails are hopelessly relegated to playing “catch up” in a seemingly eternal regulatory lag (RegLag) even during periods when deregulatory forces are muted. This article examines how data, more practically big data, is the current and the likely future consumable feeding ML. AI’s hallucinations and deserved reputation for mistakes likely is attenuated with carefully designed deployments of more and more data sensing mechanisms that respond to various stimuli. These include potentiometers, transducers, electrodes, receptors, optical array, acoustic and other emerging technologies that actuate modern sensor data streams. AI’s “black box” opacity may eventually yield to a new transparency as fusion or integration of sensor data from multiple sources serves to produce more consistent, accurate and reliable findings that leave durable audit trails. Meteorology seems a widely understood multi-sensor discipline, it serves as an ideal context to generalize policy-makers understanding of how diverse sensor deployments feed prediction models. Meteorologists commonly accept geographically dispersed sensor readings of ambient temperature, barometric pressure, wind speed/direction, humidity, and progressive imagery from cameras, radar and satellites. All such sensors are susceptible to error from noise, resolution, calibration durability and data compilation (in)frequency. This article examines the promise and policy challenges of multi sensor data fusion (MSDF)4 where data is obtained from various sources, analog vs. digital, sounds and images, mechanical/electronic instrument readings, and natural language text. Considerable MSDF data is synthetic, artificially generated by algorithms to train, validate and modify models. MSDF is increasingly used directly in control systems, often without much, if any, human intervention. Many AI deployments demand validation by modeling their evolving algorithms to integrate data from diverse sources with an aim to: (i) improve decision-making quality, (ii) verify initial and evolving conclusions in the truth-discovery process, and (iii) rate, weight and rank authenticity and reliability of particular sensor designs, sensor placement locations, phenomena measurement sensitivities, evaluation of sensor impairment results, latency and various dependability measures. MSDF is a scientific measurement field that has been useful for years in geospatial (GIS) and bioinformatics application domains. However, as AI is deployed in many other domains, MSDF will usher in sufficient public policy impacts, such that MSDF expertise will become increasingly useful to lawmakers, judges, regulators, expert witnesses, and litigator’s, none of whom can afford to ignore MSDF. This article argues and demonstrates that MSDF cannot be ceded to the experts. As in other technical fields, the scientific aspects of MSDF networks will drive litigation issue resolution as well as public policy analysis.

Discover the Many Dimensions of Meditation: Ancient Wisdom, Modern Science, and Everything In Between

Explore the frontier where mindfulness meets mysticism and discover the practice that can change your mind, your life, and the world around you.

title: Green Finance and the Circular Economy Transition: Policy Frameworks, Financial Instruments, and Impact Metrics
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Green Finance and the Circular Economy Transition: Policy Frameworks, Financial Instruments, and Impact Metrics
detail.abstract: This study synthesizes research and policy analysis on how green finance can enable the shift from linear production models to circular economic systems. It outlines core principles, additionality, transparency, targeted use-of-proceeds, and ESG integration, and maps financial instruments (green bonds, sustainability-linked bonds and loans, sustainable banking products, blended finance, impact equity, and public–private partnerships) to circular activities such as advanced recycling, remanufacturing, product-as-a-service, and regenerative land management. Key stakeholder roles are identified across banks, institutional investors, development finance institutions, standard-setters, firms, civil society, and technology providers. Regulatory and market enablers discussed include taxonomies, mandatory disclosure, Extended Producer Responsibility, carbon pricing, and procurement policies that create demand certainty. Technological enablers, IoT monitoring, blockchain traceability, and digital marketplaces, improve measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) and reduce information asymmetries. Barriers highlighted include perceived project risk, lack of standardized metrics, volatile secondary-material markets, and limited SME access to capital. The analysis concludes that aligning finance contracts with measurable circular KPIs, deploying blended risk-sharing mechanisms, strengthening MRV and taxonomy harmonization, and building institutional capacity are essential to scale investment that delivers economic, climate, and biodiversity benefits.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the ethical and legal implications of public officials, elected representatives, and high-profile personalities attending celebratory or fundraising events organized by parties engaged in ongoing litigation. The analysis considers potential indirect influence on litigation outcomes, the risk of perceived or actual bias, and the alignment of resources in support of one party. Drawing analogies to third-party litigation funding and charitable asset diversion, the paper argues that even seemingly benign participation may raise legitimate concerns under administrative law, Charter fairness principles, and nonprofit governance frameworks. The objective is to frame a systematic discussion for policymakers, legal practitioners, and courts, highlighting the need for guidelines, disclosure obligations, and risk management in such scenarios.

detail.title: Agentic AI vs. Generative AI: A Combined Approach for Financial Compliance
detail.abstract: This article evaluates the combined use of Agentic AI and Generative AI in managing financial compliance. The introduction of Agentic AI works with goalorientation and autonomous systems to empower the financial compliance needs. This helps to handle transaction monitoring and fraud detection needs. On the other hand, using Generative AI works to assist in managing regulatory texts, ensuring that a combination of the two can work towards achieving a flawless mechanism of handling reasoning, auditability, adaptability and cost efficiency in addressing compliance needs. Thus, these approaches advance a modest way to cater for the requirements of advancing security. The article provides a case study of working with KYC compliance, handling economic impacts, management of RegTech markets and providing financial oversight to ensure that there is a flawless management of the combined use of Agentic and Generative AI in financial compliance.

title: China's Soft Power Diplomacy in International Politics: Strategies, Means and Implications
affiliations: and Galgotias University

detail.title: China's Soft Power Diplomacy in International Politics: Strategies, Means and Implications
detail.abstract: The concept of soft power has become increasingly significant in the realm of international politics. As nations seek to exert their influence on the global stage, the ability to shape the preferences and perceptions of others through non-coercive means has emerged as a vital tool. China, with its rapidly growing economic and political clout, has substantially engaged in exercising strategies and means as soft power politics to accomplish its presence in the global politics. This research paper examines China's soft power diplomacy in international politics, focusing on the strategies and means employed by the Chinese government to enhance its global influence. The primary objective of this research is to investigate how China strategically employs soft power and assess the implications of these strategies on international politics. To achieve this, the study utilizes a qualitative approach, considering key indicators such as culture, diplomacy, education, and public opinion. By examining China's soft power initiatives and their effects, this research sheds light on the evolving dynamics of international politics in the 21st century, where soft power plays a significant role in shaping global perceptions and relations

title: Artificial Intelligence, Human Intelligence and Corporate Governance
affiliations: University of Louisiana at Lafayette and ISG Paris

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Human Intelligence and Corporate Governance
detail.abstract:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into corporate governance has begun to redefine how organizations operate and make strategic decisions. This study explores this integration of AI into corporate governance using a unique approach: more than 30 corporate governance experts were surveyed to obtain their diverse, expert perspectives on this issue. 

These corporate governance experts approached the future of AI and corporate governance from four distinct perspectives: cultural dimensions, venture governance, family firm governance and social impact governance. Despite working on vastly different research agendas, several common themes emerged from these contributors. Boards and executives are increasingly using AI tools for analytics, predictive modeling, and risk management, creating opportunities to enhance decision-making and transparency. However, this technological shift brings new challenges, including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, and ethical accountability. Corporate governance has always been a uniquely human function, whether that entails making decisions in the board room, creating governance systems and policies or debating shareholder proposals. Will AI allow these humans to serve their governance functions more efficiently and effectively or will it interfere with the rational, context-based decision-making that only humans provide? This paper studies the role of AI in corporate governance, focusing on the intersection of human beings exercising their human intelligence and technology-enhanced artificial intelligence and how AI can both enhance corporate governance and potentially compromise corporate governance.

title: Geopolitical Turmoil, Supply-Chain Realignment, and Inflation: Commodity Shocks, Trade Fragmentation, and Policy Responses
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Geopolitical Turmoil, Supply-Chain Realignment, and Inflation: Commodity Shocks, Trade Fragmentation, and Policy Responses
detail.abstract: This analysis synthesizes theoretical frameworks and empirical evidence to trace how geopolitical tensions propagate through supply chains, commodity markets, and financial channels into domestic price dynamics. It identifies short-run cost-push pathways, energy and food shocks, shipping disruptions, and exchange-rate depreciation, and maps longer-run structural effects from trade realignment, reshoring, and increased supplier concentration. Differential exposures across advanced and emerging economies are highlighted, including stronger pass-through via import dependence and constrained policy space in frontier markets. Sectoral assessment of energy, agriculture, and technology shows how concentrated production, export controls, and logistical chokepoints amplify volatility and disrupt industrial production. Policy responses examined include monetary adjustments (interest-rate management, flexible inflation anchors, and FX tools), fiscal measures (targeted subsidies and strategic investment), trade instruments (diversion and facilitation), and multilateral cooperation (liquidity support, coordinated corridors, and reserve sharing). Scenario analysis explores escalation risks and compound shocks, and proposes resilience strategies: diversified sourcing, regional integration, strategic stockpiles, and investment in alternative energy and processing capacity. The findings indicate that political fragmentation elevates baseline costs and that integrated, cross-sector policy packages are necessary to limit persistent inflationary pressures while preserving growth.

title: Synergy Over Spiral: A Logistics 5.0 Game-Theoretic Model for Trust-Fatigue Co-regulation in Human-Cobot Order Picking
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kharagpur - Department of Industrial Engineering and Management and Rashtreeya Vidyalaya College of Engineering (RVCE)

detail.title: Synergy Over Spiral: A Logistics 5.0 Game-Theoretic Model for Trust-Fatigue Co-regulation in Human-Cobot Order Picking
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the critical role of trust and fatigue in human-cobot collaborative order picking, framing the challenge within the scope of Logistics 5.0: the implementation of human-robot symbiosis in smart logistics. We propose a dynamic, leader-follower Stackelberg game to model this interaction, where utility functions explicitly account for human fatigue and trust. Through agentbased simulations, we demonstrate that while a naive model leads to a "trust death spiral," a refined trust model creates a "trust synergy cycle," increasing productivity by nearly 100%. Finally, we show that a cobot operating in a Trust-Recovery Mode can overcome system brittleness after a disruption, reducing trust recovery time by over 75% compared to a non-adaptive model. Our findings provide a framework for designing intelligent cobot behaviors that fulfill the Industry 5.0 pillars of human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience.

title: Saving the Literary Commons: Meanjin, Governance Friction, and the Call for Stewardship
affiliations: James Cook University - College of Business, Law and Governance,

detail.title: Saving the Literary Commons: Meanjin, Governance Friction, and the Call for Stewardship
detail.abstract: The announced closure of Meanjin, Australia's second-oldest literary journal, exposes deeper structural tensions in the governance of culture. While justified on "financial grounds," this decision reflects a wider drift in universities from cultural stewardship toward budgetary rationalism. Framed through the lens of commons theory, the paper repositions literary journals as civic infrastructure, sites of reciprocity, circulation, and imagination rather than commodities. Drawing on Ostrom, Hyde, and Yúdice, it situates Meanjin's fate within broader shifts of commodification and erosion of the cultural public sphere. The analysis applies the Governance Friction Continuum (Harmony → Friction → Conflict → Collapse) to demonstrate how drift hardened into rupture, and how public dissent functions as a form of governance intervention. The paper calls for literary foundations and philanthropic trusts to act as structural stewards, advancing new models of platform stewardship to secure long-term viability. Ultimately, the closure of Meanjin signals both a crisis and an opportunity: to reconstitute the literary commons through imagination, solidarity, and governance attuned to the logics of the gift.

title: Transit Design, Transportation Policy and Location-Mode Choice in the Era of Telework
affiliations: Northwestern University and Northwestern University

detail.title: Transit Design, Transportation Policy and Location-Mode Choice in the Era of Telework
detail.abstract: This study develops an analytical framework to examine how telework affects commuting mode choice, residential location patterns, and urban transit policy. We incorporate user heterogeneity and multi-modality-transit, driving, and telework-into a monocentric city model, upon which a bi-level transit design problem featuring both utilitarian and egalitarian objectives is formulated. Using the model, we characterize the location-mode joint equilibrium and analyze how transit design and financial levers shape outcomes. Analytical results reveal a distinct sorting pattern: lower-income residents locate closer to the central business district and choose public transit, middle-income residents drive from mid-range suburbs, and higher-income residents opt for telework from the periphery, where spatial mixing occurs due to location indifference among teleworkers. A case study of a Chicago commuter corridor confirms these patterns and shows that the post-pandemic uptick in telework results in uneven welfare gains across income levels. We also find that redesigning transit service-particularly increasing stop spacing to improve operational efficiency-and adopting fare-free transit significantly improve social welfare, especially for low-income commuters. By contrast, taxation or congestion tolls yields limited additional benefits. Taken together, these findings highlight how changes in work behavior interact with residential and travel choices, and underscore the need to rethink related public policies in the era of telework.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes AML risks in extraordinary finance transactions, focusing on M&A and corporate restructurings, and shows how valuation discretion (DCF assumptions, peer multiples, purchase price allocation/goodwill) can be exploited for money-laundering schemes and value transfers. It proposes an Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) checklist and a risk-scoring model with quantitative thresholds (acquisition premium vs. sector median, goodwill-to-enterprise-value ratio, DCF sensitivity), illustrated with practical examples and protected through contractual safeguards.

title: The Post-Hegemonic World Order: Beyond U.S.–China Rivalry

detail.title: The Post-Hegemonic World Order: Beyond U.S.–China Rivalry
detail.abstract:
This article challenges the dominant narrative of hegemonic bipolarity in international relations, arguing that the global order is no longer defined by the strategic rivalry between the United States and China. Instead, it is increasingly shaped by fragmented, issue-specific coalitions that reflect a decentralized and networked distribution of power. While the U.S.–China framework continues to dominate policy discourse and academic analysis, it oversimplifies the complexity of contemporary global dynamics and marginalizes the agency of regional powers, non-state actors, and transnational networks.

The paper critiques the historical legacy of bipolarity and its theoretical reproduction in current IR scholarship, using post-structuralist and critical realist approaches to deconstruct binary logic. It then introduces the concept of “networked multipolarity,” a framework that emphasizes relational power, strategic hedging, and normative entrepreneurship. Through empirical case studies in climate diplomacy, digital governance, security coalitions, and trade alliances, the article demonstrates how actors form overlapping coalitions based on shared interests rather than ideological alignment. The final sections explore the strategic implications of this shift for global governance, highlighting both the opportunities and risks of fragmentation. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for states, institutions, scholars, and civil society, and calls for a paradigm shift in international relations theory—one that reflects the fluidity, complexity, and pluralism of the emerging global order.

title: Guns, Lawyers, and Markets: On Economic and Political Consequences of Costly Conflict
affiliations: University of California - Department of Economics and Deakin University - School of Accounting, Economics and Finance

detail.title: Guns, Lawyers, and Markets: On Economic and Political Consequences of Costly Conflict
detail.abstract: We synthesize research on conflict as a fundamental economic phenomenon, arguing that the implications of the ”dark side of self-interest” have received insufficient attention in economics. We define conflict as interactions where parties choose costly inputs that are adversarially combined against one another — distinct from the collaborative input combinations typical in economic models. We make four key contributions: First, we demonstrate that conflict induces economically significant costs comparable to or exceeding traditional deadweight losses. Second, we explain how these costs vary across contexts based on property rights protection, state capacity, and cultural norms. Third, we show how incorporating conflict into economic models leads to substantially different predictions than traditional models — including inverse relationships between compensation and productivity; distortions in comparative advantage; prices determined by power rather than solely by preferences endowments, and technology. Fourth, attributes of modern states such as centralization in the presence of law, checks and balances, other forms of distributed power, and the bureaucratic form of organization can partly be thought of as restraining conflict and appropriation, with implications for governance and economic development. Overall, in the presence of conflict and appropriation, power considerations cannot be separated from economics and first-best models are not empirically plausible.

title: Battery Talent Census Report: Skills, Training, and Growth Insights from 1,000 Battery Professionals
affiliations: University of Michigan - Department of Mechanical Engineering

detail.title: Battery Talent Census Report: Skills, Training, and Growth Insights from 1,000 Battery Professionals
detail.abstract: The battery industry has become foundational to the global energy transition and a linchpin of U.S. industrial competitiveness. The lithium-ion battery chain is positioned for extraordinary growth, potentially reaching a value of more than $400 billion by 2030. Beyond electric mobility and grid storage, new frontiers, ranging from electric aviation to AI data centers and defense, further amplify the strategic importance of batteries in the coming decades. Realizing the growth potential of the battery industry, however, requires addressing a fundamental constraint: talent shortages. The battery industry's rate of expansion is directly limited by workforce availability. Advancing ongoing conversations around workforce planning requires a clear understanding of the current state of the workforce. Until now, conversations about battery talent gaps have been dominated by anecdotes and fragmented surveys. The Battery Talent Census, based on responses from over 1,000 industry professionals, provides the most comprehensive, data-driven snapshot of skilled knowledge workers powering the battery sector to date. This report presents the full results of the Census, covering everything from demographic insights on today's battery professionals to the skills and roles most in demand, evolving compensation and retention dynamics, and how students view their future career pathways. Recognizing that different audiences will prioritize different insights, we distill our key findings and recommendations into four stakeholder groups: educational institutions and content creators; students and job seekers; battery company leaders and recruiters; and policymakers.

title: Corporate Crime in European Emerging Markets
affiliations: Okinawa University and Charles University in Prague - Institute of Economic Studies

detail.title: Corporate Crime in European Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: We examine the corporate criminal records of 18,187 firms operating in 17 European emerging markets and empirically analyze the effects of board composition and national institutions on crime deterrence. Our analysis reveals that 872 firms (about 5% of the sample) committed 1,734 crimes over 2020-2023. We show that firms with larger boards and greater board independence are associated with higher incidences of corporate crime, suggesting that larger or nominally independent boards may not function effectively in emerging market contexts. In contrast, female leadership and board gender diversity do not exhibit significant deterrent effects, implying that gender inclusion alone may not suffice in these environments. In banks with an outside board chairman, the occurrence of corporate crime increases substantially. Importantly, stronger national institutions consistently correlate with lower crime rates, a pattern observed universally across European emerging markets, and boards in countries with stronger institutions appear more effective in deterring crime

title: Workplace Peer Effects in Fertility Decisions
affiliations: Università degli Studi della Calabria - Department of Economics and Statistics, Department of Economics and Statistics (DiSES), University of Naples Federico II and Università degli Studi della Calabria - Department of Economics and Statistics

detail.title: Workplace Peer Effects in Fertility Decisions
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of co-workers’ fertility on individual fertility decisions. Using matched employer-employee data from Italian social security records (2016–2020), we estimate how fertility among co-workers of similar age and occupation affects the individual likelihood of having a child. We exploit variation introduced by the 2015 Jobs Act, which reduced fertility among workers hired under weaker employment protection. Focusing on workers hired before the reform and using the share of colleagues hired after the reform as an instrument for peer fertility, we find that a one-percentage-point increase in peer fertility raises individual fertility by 0.4 percentage points (a 10% increase). Heterogeneity analysis suggests that while social influence and social norms are key mechanisms, information sharing and career concerns, particularly among women, tend to moderate the response. Our findings highlight how changes in employment protection may have unintended fertility spillovers through workplace social interactions.

title: From open to closed societies: Inequality, migration, and women's rights
affiliations: LUMSA University, University of Bologna and Institute for Advanced Study In Toulouse (IAST)

detail.title: From open to closed societies: Inequality, migration, and women's rights
detail.abstract: We study six centuries of institutional change in the governance of the commons across over three hundred Italian communities. Wealthier communities, facing migration pressure due to unequal resource endowments, restricted access to common property resources by excluding women from membership, thereby limiting migration through marriage. Using archival data and an agent-based model, we show that this endogenous closure spread via a domino effect and persisted until a centralized Napoleonic reform reinstated egalitarian access. The findings highlight how migration, inequality, and gendered institutions interact in polycentric systems, offering broader insights for the political economy of property rights on land and institutional reform in developing contexts.

title: Globalization and Gender Equality
affiliations: Ifo Institute, , Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) and KOF Swiss Economic Institute, ETH Zurich

detail.title: Globalization and Gender Equality
detail.abstract: Globalization and Gender Equality Legal rights continue to differ between women and men, particularly in developing countries. In this paper, we examine whether economic integration can improve gender equality by law. We design a novel instrumental variable strategy based on regional waves of globalization, which serve as strong exogenous predictors of national globalization trends. Our main estimate suggests that an increase of one-third in the globalization index, equivalent to a permanent transition from Indonesia to the United States, is associated with a 12.1% increase in gender equality, measured by the extent to which men and women are treated equally by law. We also find that this effect is almost entirely driven by de facto globalization. Linking globalization to more than 300,000 individuals from about 100 countries, we provide evidence for a microfoundation of the macroeconomic effects.

title: Replacing What Could Be Repaired: A Structural Analysis of Two-Stage Diagnostic Decisions in Managing Shared-Bike Returns
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Carlson School of Management, Temple University-Fox School of Business and Temple University - Department of Statistics, Operations, and Data Science

detail.title: Replacing What Could Be Repaired: A Structural Analysis of Two-Stage Diagnostic Decisions in Managing Shared-Bike Returns
detail.abstract: Bike-sharing platforms face significant challenges from high maintenance costs, driven by heavy usage and inefficiencies in diagnostic decision-making. Using task-level data from a leading bike-sharing platform, we develop a structural estimation model to analyze two-stage diagnostic decisions made by inspectors (stage 1) and workers (stage 2). These decisions are modeled as a strategic interaction governed by a Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE). To address the computational complexity of Maximum Likelihood Estimation with BNE constraints, we employ machine learning to approximate BNE. We identify systematic overtreatment tendencies among inspectors and workers, resulting in a higher false positive rate than that under the firm's optimal decisions and thus inflating maintenance costs. Our counterfactual analyses show that higher part costs, reducing workers' piece-rate wages, adopting structured job matching, and prioritizing worker training can substantially reduce costs. Transitioning from a two-stage to a one-stage process lowers diagnostic accuracy and increases costs, although optimizing wages narrows this gap. This framework provides actionable insights for mitigating inefficiencies in multi-agent diagnostic decision systems and is generalizable to other credence goods industries, such as heavy equipment maintenance and healthcare, where diagnostic errors have significant financial, operational, and health implications.

title: "Will the Circle Be Unbroken": The Role of Law School Centers in Advancing Restorative Justice Theory, Practice, and Education
affiliations: University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law

detail.title: "Will the Circle Be Unbroken": The Role of Law School Centers in Advancing Restorative Justice Theory, Practice, and Education

publicationDetails.detailsText: U of Maryland Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-11
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Academic centers offer unique opportunities for law schools to advance restorative justice through a combination of teaching, research, and community-engaged
practice. Centers serve as incubators to study and teach restorative justice and put theory into practice through law clinics and direct community service. As academic hubs, centers can facilitate an interactive dialogue or “unbroken circle” connecting restorative justice education, scholarship, and practice. Each aspect of the trifecta enhances the others: Restorative justice work in the community provides practical insights and informs research and teaching. In turn, scholarship and teaching sharpen and amplify community-based models. Teaching provides a platform to incorporate emerging scholarship and examples of restorative justice work.

This article examines this dialogic relationship among restorative justice teaching, scholarship, and community practice through the lens of the evolution of the Center for Dispute Resolution at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law (C-DRUM) over two decades. C-DRUM started its restorative work as part of a conflict resolution education program in K-12 Maryland schools. That community-based restorative work grew and expanded into the law school curriculum, providing both traditional classroom and experiential opportunities for law students. Over time, the guiding principles of restorative justice—including the centering of relationships and community-based processes to promote accountability and repair harm—broadened C-DRUM’s mission and influenced the center’s other work.

title: Constitutional Dimensions of Environmental Jurisprudence in India: An Analysis
affiliations: Guru Nanak Dev University and Guru Nanak Dev University

detail.title: Constitutional Dimensions of Environmental Jurisprudence in India: An Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Indian Constitution: Changing Paradigms, Pp. 114-125, Pacific Books International

detail.abstract: This study undertakes a doctrinal jurisprudential analysis of evolving environmental constitutionalism, with a particular emphasis on the Triveni Sangam framework, an integrative schema comprising Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), and Fundamental Duties. Situated against the backdrop of India’s post-Stockholm legal transformations, this research fills a critical gap in literature that often isolates these constitutional components rather than examining their synergistic interplay. The principal objective is to investigate how judicial interpretation has operationalised environmental mandates in the absence of robust legislative frameworks. This study maps the constitutional trajectory of landmark decisions from Subhash Kumar to Hanuman Laxman Aroskar. It highlights the role of judiciary in upholding salus populi suprema lex. Preliminary results reveal that the Supreme Court has consistently expanded the ambit of Art. 21 to include the right to a pollution-free environment. The precautionary principle and polluter pays doctrine strengthen enforcement. The 42nd Amendment’s insertion of Articles 48A and 51A(g) has further enabled judicial innovation, allowing courts to construct a composite eco-centric jurisprudence. Promising findings underscore that the judiciary’s use of locus standi expansion and interpretive harmonisation has compensated for legislative inertia, thereby reinforcing sustainability as a constitutional imperative. The implications are manifold. The study demonstrates how constitutional courts act as ecological sentinels, transforming aspirational provisions into enforceable rights. This research not only contributes to comparative constitutional environmentalism but also provides normative scaffolding for embedding environmental justice within Global South legal systems. This marks a significant doctrinal advance in green constitutional theory.

detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the 1989 WMUZ Detroit debate between John P. Koster and Frank R. Zindler as a test of explanatory adequacy. It asks which model-mindless matter or an organizing Mind-better accounts for three facts: (L) the law-like regularity of nature, (F) life-permitting fine-tuning, and (C) the rise of consciousness. Koster leaned on scripture without operational clarity, while Zindler stressed burden of proof but lacked a unifying model. By applying an evidence-from-effects method, this study proposes a decision rule: the preferred explanation is whichever framework coherently unifies L+F+C with fewer assumptions. Why 2025? The core issues raised in 1989-definition, evidence, and method-remain, but the stakes are clearer: debates now hinge on explanatory adequacy across physics-like lawfulness, fine-tuning discussions, and the philosophy of mind. This reply updates the frame to a practical test anyone can apply explain the whole bundle (L+F+C) with minimal assumptions-or concede that a single intelligent cause better unifies what otherwise fragments into ad-hoc patches. title: Missing Markets for Innovation: Evidence from New Uses of Existing Drugs
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Stanford University, Independent Researcher and Dartmouth College

detail.title: Missing Markets for Innovation: Evidence from New Uses of Existing Drugs

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-125
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: For large classes of potential inventions, intellectual property rights that are available on paper are either not possible or not profitable for firms to enforce in practice. In this paper, we show that these missing incentives yield quantitatively significant underinvestment in research and development. We develop a simple model that formalizes the conditions under which such missing markets for innovation arise. We identify an empirical setting-research into new uses for existing drugs-in which there is sharp variation in the enforceability of intellectual property rights on otherwise comparable inventions over time. We show that when intellectual property rights become unenforceable, research investment and commercialization nearly cease. In doing so, we test two claims central both to our model and the innovation literature more generally-that stronger intellectual property protection does, in fact, induce investment, and that heterogeneity in the availability of these rights distorts investment. The welfare consequences of inadequate incentives in our empirical context are large. Our estimates suggest that 200-800 new uses for existing drugs would have been developed under counterfactual policies. Measures of the value of these uses drawn from existing literature suggest that the social cost of this particular missing market is on the order of several trillion dollars.
